passages.happening:
Israel goes out to fight the Philistines, camping at Ebenezer while the Philistines camp at Aphek. Israel is beaten, and about four thousand men die on the field (verses 1-2).

The elders ask the question they should ask, and then answer it the wrong way. “Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, so that it may go with us to save us from the hand of our enemies” (verse 3).

So the ark is brought from Shiloh, ‘the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim’, and with it come Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas (verse 4). When it enters the camp, Israel raises a shout that shakes the ground (verse 5).

The Philistines hear it and are afraid. “The gods have entered their camp!” they said. “Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before” (verse 7). They remember the gods who struck the Egyptians, and they urge one another to fight like men or become slaves to the Hebrews (verses 8-9).

They fight, and Israel is crushed. Each man flees to his tent, and thirty thousand foot soldiers fall (verse 10). “The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The Philistines had settled on the southern coastal plain early in the twelfth century BC, and by now they were pushing into the hill country where Israel lived. Aphek is usually placed at the springs of the Yarkon River, at the edge of the coastal plain, a natural place to gather an army before moving inland. Ebenezer lay nearby in the foothills. Some archaeologists have proposed that a small Iron Age village called Izbet Sartah, where one of the earliest alphabet inscriptions in the region was found, was Ebenezer, but that is not certain.

The ark of the covenant was a wooden chest overlaid with gold, holding the tablets of the covenant. Its lid, between the cherubim, was seen as the throne of the invisible LORD. In Israel's early days the ark had gone before the people in the wilderness and at Jericho.

Ancient peoples often carried the images or signs of their gods into battle, believing that a god's presence would win the day. The elders treat the ark the same way, as a device that will make God fight for them. They never ask whether he wants to. In this book the problem is not that Israel serves another god here. It treats the LORD's own ark as if it were an idol.

The Philistines speak of gods in the plural, and they mix up the plagues of Egypt with the wilderness. It is a garbled memory of the exodus, but a real one. Their fear makes them fight harder.

The numbers, four thousand and thirty thousand, raise a question asked elsewhere in these books. Some scholars think the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit or a clan's company, which would make the numbers smaller. Others take them as they stand.
passages.later:
When the ark set out in the wilderness, Moses had prayed, “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You” (Numbers 10:35). The elders want that prayer answered without the faithfulness that went with it.

A psalm remembers this day as God's own judgment: “He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men. He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary” (Psalm 78:60-61).
passages.hard:
Why would God let his own ark be captured by people who did not worship him?

The capture seems to shame God before the nations, and Israel certainly felt it that way. The story answers in stages. First, it is judgment. The priests who carried the ark were corrupt, and the people were using God instead of seeking him, so what the man of God and Samuel had announced now happens: both sons die on one day (2:34). Second, the capture exposes a false belief, that God's presence could be carried like a lucky charm and would bring victory no matter how Israel lived. Third, the next chapters show that God was not defeated. In chapter 5 the ark humbles the Philistine god Dagon and brings plague on the Philistine towns until they send it back.

Many readers see in this a pattern found throughout Scripture, where God allows what looks like defeat to do what people cannot see. Others stress that the text refuses to soften the loss. The ark never returns to Shiloh, and the priesthood there never recovers.
passages.asks: The elders asked why they had lost, and then reached for the ark instead of turning to God. Ask what you reach for when things go wrong: a habit, a ritual, a holy object, a familiar prayer said like a charm. And ask what it would mean to seek God himself rather than something that stands for him.

passages.happening:
That same day a man of Benjamin runs from the battle line all the way to Shiloh, ‘with his clothes torn and dirt on his head’ (verse 12).

Eli is sitting on his chair beside the road, watching, ‘because his heart trembled for the ark of God’ (verse 13). The man enters the city with his report, and the whole city cries out. Eli hears the noise and asks what it means (verse 14). He is ninety-eight years old, and blind (verse 15).

The messenger tells him: “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are both dead, and the ark of God has been captured” (verse 17).

“As soon as the ark of God was mentioned, Eli fell backward from his chair by the city gate, and being old and heavy, he broke his neck and died. And Eli had judged Israel forty years” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Torn clothes and dirt on the head were the usual signs of mourning and disaster. Before the runner says a word, the whole town knows the news is bad.

The narrator slows down here. He gives Eli's age, his blindness and his anxious waiting, so that the reader feels the blow land. The report comes in four steps: Israel has fled, there has been a great slaughter, your sons are dead, the ark is captured. Eli falls only at the last. What he cared about most was the ark, more even than his sons.

The word heavy is the same Hebrew root as glory and honor. In chapter 2 God charged Eli with honoring his sons more than God and with fattening himself on the offerings. Now he dies because he was heavy. Even his chair, a word that can also mean throne, recalls the first chapter, where he sat by the doorpost and misread Hannah's prayer.

Eli is called a judge. His forty years end on the day the word against his house comes true.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers the priests who died that day and the grief that could not be spoken: “His priests fell by the sword, but their widows could not lament” (Psalm 78:64).

Centuries later Jeremiah warned Jerusalem that its temple was not safe because the ark was there: ‘what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust’ (Jeremiah 7:14).
passages.asks: Eli's heart trembled for the ark, and still he had not restrained his sons. Ask whether you can care deeply about God's honor in public and still neglect what he asks of you at home. And ask what you are watching for anxiously, by the road, and whether it is what matters most.

passages.happening:
Phinehas's wife is pregnant and near her time. When she hears that the ark has been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband are dead, she goes into labor and gives birth (verse 19).

As she is dying, the women attending her try to comfort her. “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!” ‘But she did not respond or pay any heed’ (verse 20).

She names the boy Ichabod. “The glory has departed from Israel,” she said, “for the ark of God has been captured” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Naming a child for the circumstances of its birth was common. Ichabod probably means Where is the glory? or No glory. His birth becomes a memorial of the disaster.

The chapter does not end with Eli's death. It ends with a woman who is never named, and her verdict, said twice: the glory has departed. She sees more clearly than the elders did. The worst loss was not the battle, or even her husband. It was that God's presence seemed to have gone from Israel.

The verb for departed can also mean to go into exile. So her cry can be heard as the glory has gone into exile. Readers who first received the finished book, perhaps after Jerusalem had fallen to Babylon, would have heard their own story in it.

Glory in Hebrew is again the word for weight. Israel has lost the very thing that gave it weight.
passages.later: Ezekiel, in exile in Babylon, saw a vision of the glory leaving God's house in Jerusalem: “Then the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple and stood above the cherubim” (Ezekiel 10:18). Like this mother, he saw that the worst thing that could happen to God's people was for his presence to go.
passages.asks: A dying mother saw what the elders had missed: losing God's presence was worse than losing a battle. Ask what you would grieve most if it were taken away, and whether God's presence is anywhere on that list. And ask whether worship can go on in your life after the glory has quietly gone.
